CV.1.q: What does the peak reading on the meter measure?
options: How long the note has lasted
The tallest point the wave reaches
CV.1.why: Peak is the tallest point of the wave in the stretch the meter looks at.

CV.1.q: What is the average reading closest to?
options: How much sound there is over a short stretch
CV.1.why: The average is worked out from every point of the wave, so it follows how much sound there is.

CV.1.q: For a pure tone, where does the average sit compared with the peak?
CV.1.why: A pure tone always reads 3 dB between peak and average, on any note.

CV.1.q: Can the average ever read above the peak?
CV.1.why: The average is made from points that are all at or under the peak, so it cannot pass it.

CV.1.q: You turn Volume down 6 dB. What happens to the gap between peak and average?
CV.1.why: Volume changes the size of the wave and not its shape, so both readings move together.

CV.1.q: What does change the gap between the two readings?
options: Playing a different key on a pure tone
Changing the shape of the wave
CV.1.why: A wave with brief tall points has a high peak with little sound under it, so the gap depends on shape.

CV.2.q: You take 6 dB away. What happens to the height of the wave?
CV.2.why: Every 6 dB halves or doubles the height.

CV.2.q: After turning down 6 dB twice, how tall is the wave compared with the start?
CV.2.why: Two halvings make a quarter, while the decibels add up to 12.

CV.2.q: How many times shorter is a wave after a 20 dB drop?
CV.2.why: A change of 20 dB is ten times the height.

CV.2.q: What does a decibel figure always do?
CV.2.why: Decibels say how many times bigger one level is than another.

CV.2.q: Why does silence have no decibel number?
options: Nothing is not any number of times smaller than something
CV.2.why: Decibels count times, and no number of halvings ever reaches nothing.

CV.3.q: What does a level meter measure?
CV.3.why: A meter measures the wave. Loudness is what you hear.

CV.3.q: Two different sounds read the same on the meter. What can you say?
options: The lower one is always louder
They will not necessarily sound equally loud
CV.3.why: The same reading does not guarantee the same loudness.

CV.3.q: In the lesson, how did the meter read for the very low note and the very high note?
CV.3.why: A pure tone on this synth has the same level on every key, whatever it sounds like to you.

CV.3.q: You turn one sound up by about 3 dB. What is fairly reliable?
options: It sounds about one step louder
CV.3.why: A change of about 3 dB to one sound is about one step in loudness.

CV.3.q: What is the meter best used for?
options: Ranking two different sounds by loudness
Comparing a sound with itself as you change it
CV.3.why: Use the meter for changes to one sound and your ears to compare different sounds.

CV.4.q: Two identical waves play exactly in step. How much does the level rise over one alone?
CV.4.why: In step they make one wave twice as tall, and twice as tall is 6 dB.

CV.4.q: The same two waves are set half a cycle apart. What does the meter read?
CV.4.why: Every rise in one meets an equal fall in the other, so they cancel.

CV.4.q: Two oscillators play different notes at the same level. How much does the average rise over one alone?
CV.4.why: Unrelated sounds line up only some of the time, so on average they add 3 dB.

CV.4.q: With two different notes, why can the peak still reach 6 dB up?
options: The notes get louder over time
At some instants the two waves line up
CV.4.why: The peak catches the instants when both waves are high together.

CV.4.q: Two oscillators a few cents apart make the meter swing. Why?
options: They drift in and out of step
CV.4.why: They pass through in step, then opposite, over and over: 6 dB up, then nearly nothing.

options: Which tones a sound is made of
CV.5.why: The scope shows the shape of the wave over time.

options: Which tones the wave is made of and how strong each is
CV.5.why: The spectrum is a list of ingredients: the tones and their strengths.

CV.5.q: You slide one of two tones in time. What happens?
options: The scope's shape changes and the spectrum stays put
The spectrum changes and the scope stays put
CV.5.why: The same tones can add up to many shapes, depending on how they line up.

CV.5.q: When the shape changed but the ingredients did not, what did the meter do?
options: The average moved and the peak did not
The peak moved a little and the average did not
CV.5.why: The peak follows the shape. The average follows the ingredients.

CV.6.q: On the spectrogram, which way does time run?
options: Left to right, newest on the right
Right to left, newest on the left
CV.6.why: Time runs left to right, with the newest sound on the right.

CV.6.q: What does a stronger colour mean?
CV.6.why: Pitch runs bottom to top, and stronger colour means louder.

CV.6.q: What does a steady held note look like?
CV.6.why: Each harmonic draws its own level stripe for as long as the note lasts.

options: A slope from left to right
CV.6.why: Stripes mean harmonics. Noise has none, so it fills the whole height.

CV.6.q: Why do the stripes crowd together toward the top?
options: Each octave gets equal height on this picture
CV.6.why: Harmonics are evenly spaced in frequency, and here each octave takes the same height.

CV.7.q: What is a jump in a wave?
CV.7.why: A jump is a sudden change in height. A corner is a sudden change in direction.

CV.7.q: Which shape has corners but no jumps?
CV.7.why: A triangle changes direction twice per cycle and never jumps.

CV.7.q: Why are a saw and a square both bright?
A saw's tenth harmonic is how strong compared with its first?
CV.7.why: With a jump, harmonics weaken only in proportion to their number.

options: It has only corners, which make weak high harmonics
CV.7.why: Corners make harmonics that fall away with the square of their number.

CV.7.q: What does a sine have above its first harmonic?
CV.7.why: A sine has no jump and no corner, so it has no harmonics above the first.

CV.8.q: What does a band-pass filter with high resonance let through?
options: A narrow band and very little else
CV.8.why: That narrow band is what lets you listen to one place in the sound at a time.

CV.8.q: You sweep the narrow band slowly up a steady saw. What do you hear?
CV.8.why: Each step is one harmonic passing under the band.

CV.8.q: When does the meter jump during the sweep?
options: When the band sits on a harmonic
When the band is between harmonics
CV.8.why: The level jumps on a harmonic and sinks between them.

CV.8.q: Where do a note's harmonics sit?
options: At whole-number multiples of the note
CV.8.why: Harmonics are at two, three, four times the note's frequency, and so on.

CV.8.q: Why switch the slope to Steep for this?
options: Two filter stages separate neighbouring harmonics better
CV.8.why: Two stages in a row let less of the neighbours leak through.
